description: Palmer Raids, Sacco and Vanzetti, the National Origins Act — how 1920s America closed its doors.
content_html:
Fear of Radicals: The Red Scare

In the aftermath of the First World War and the Bolshevik Revolution in Russia, a wave of anxiety about Communist and anarchist subversion swept the United States. In 1919, a series of mail bombs targeting government officials — including a device sent to Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer — and a bomb explosion outside Palmer’s home in June 1919 intensified demands for action against radicals. The result was one of the most significant attacks on civil liberties in American peacetime history.

Key Fact

The Palmer Raids took place in two main waves: November 1919 and January 1920. In the January raids alone, around 10,000 people were arrested across 33 cities. Many were held for days without charges. Evidence was often minimal or fabricated. Several hundred people, mostly foreign-born, were deported to the Soviet Union. The head of the Bureau of Investigation’s General Intelligence Division, J. Edgar Hoover, compiled files on thousands of suspected radicals. He would go on to lead the FBI for the next five decades.

The Sacco and Vanzetti Case

In April 1920, two Italian-born anarchists, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, were arrested for the murder of a paymaster and his guard during a robbery in South Braintree, Massachusetts. Their trial in 1921 became a cause célèbre. Critics argued that the prosecution was driven by their immigrant background and political beliefs rather than the evidence. The judge, Webster Thayer, made comments about the defendants’ politics that suggested prejudice.

Despite international protests — demonstrations were held in Europe, South America, and across the United States — both men were executed on 23 August 1927. In 1977, Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis issued a proclamation declaring that Sacco and Vanzetti had been unfairly tried and condemning the atmosphere of prejudice that had surrounded the case. Their guilt has been debated for a century: ballistics evidence later analysed in the 1980s suggested Sacco’s gun may have been used, while Vanzetti’s guilt appears even less certain. Present their case as procedurally flawed rather than asserting innocence as established fact.

A more permanent expression of nativist sentiment was the National Origins Act of 1924, also known as the Johnson-Reed Act. It set immigration quotas at 2 per cent of each nationality’s presence in the 1890 census — a year chosen deliberately because it pre-dated the mass immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe. The effect was to sharply reduce immigration from Italy, Poland, Russia, and other countries, while largely preserving immigration from Britain and Western Europe. Immigration from Asian countries was effectively banned entirely. The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 had already begun this process; the 1924 act made it permanent and stricter.

Responses: NAACP and UNIA

The spec for this lesson also requires knowledge of attempts to combat prejudice. The NAACP, led by James Weldon Johnson as executive secretary from 1920 to 1930, campaigned tirelessly for federal anti-lynching legislation and challenged segregation through the courts. Its magazine The Crisis, edited by W.E.B. Du Bois, reached a circulation of around 100,000 by the early 1920s, documenting racial violence and intellectual Black life.

Key Fact

Marcus Garvey’s UNIA offered a separatist vision: Black economic self-sufficiency, pride in African heritage, and ultimately the creation of an independent Black nation in Africa. Garvey’s movement attracted millions of followers in the early 1920s, particularly among working-class African Americans in northern cities. Du Bois and the NAACP were deeply critical of Garvey’s separatism, which they saw as accepting rather than challenging racial inequality. Garvey was convicted of mail fraud in 1925 and deported to Jamaica in 1927, ending his American movement.

The Palmer Raids were eventually halted by a combination of legal challenges and political embarrassment. Assistant Secretary of Labor Louis Post cancelled thousands of deportation orders on due-process grounds. By 1920, Palmer’s prediction of a major Communist revolution on May Day had proved completely wrong, damaging his credibility. The American Civil Liberties Union, founded in 1920, emerged partly in response to the abuses of the Palmer era and would go on to challenge repressive laws throughout the decade. Palmer’s hoped-for presidential run in 1920 came to nothing.
exam_tip_html: This lesson covers several distinct topics that the exam may ask about separately. When writing about Sacco and Vanzetti, always emphasise the procedural flaws (judge’s comments, climate of anti-immigrant prejudice) rather than stating they were innocent — their guilt remains debated. For the National Origins Act, make sure you know the 1924 act used the 1890 census deliberately to exclude Southern and Eastern European immigrants — that specific detail shows you understand the act’s discriminatory design. On the NAACP vs. UNIA distinction, examiners reward answers that can explain the different strategies (legal integration vs. separatist nationalism) rather than simply naming both.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Palmer Raids of 1919–20 arrested around 10,000 people in a wave of anti-Communist and anti-anarchist repression, with J. Edgar Hoover compiling intelligence files that would shape his FBI career for five decades.
  • Sacco and Vanzetti’s trial and execution in 1927 became an international symbol of anti-immigrant prejudice and a flawed justice system; the case was officially condemned as unfair by Governor Dukakis in 1977.
  • The National Origins Act of 1924 used the 1890 census to drastically cut immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe and ban Asian immigration; the NAACP and UNIA offered contrasting strategies — legal integration and separatist nationalism — in response to continued racial discrimination.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the Palmer Raids of 1919-1920.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each feature scores 1 mark for identification and 1 additional mark for specific supporting detail. Example features: mass arrests without warrants (1), with around 10,000 people detained across 33 cities in the January 1920 raids alone (1); deportation of suspected foreign-born radicals (1), including hundreds sent to the Soviet Union, demonstrating the targeting of immigrants as well as US citizens (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Sacco and Vanzetti case became an international symbol of injustice.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. the judge’s public comments suggesting prejudice against the defendants’ anarchist beliefs undermined confidence in the fairness of the trial; the immigrants’ Italian background placed them at the intersection of anti-immigrant nativism and anti-radical hysteria, making it impossible to separate their trial from the political climate of the Red Scare). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the National Origins Act of 1924 was designed to restrict immigration from particular countries.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the deliberate use of the 1890 census (pre-mass-immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe) to calculate quotas, meaning the act was specifically designed to reduce immigration from Italy, Poland, and Russia while preserving British and Western European immigration; links this to nativist ideology, economic competition fears, and the post-war xenophobia that had produced the Red Scare; notes complete ban on Asian immigration. Secure: Two or more factors explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One factor explained, others named. Emerging: General statement without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the UNIA led by Marcus Garvey.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: The UNIA promoted Black pride and African heritage (1); Garvey argued that African Americans should embrace their African identity rather than seek acceptance in a white-dominated society (1). Feature 2: The UNIA promoted economic self-sufficiency (1); Garvey established Black-owned businesses, including a steamship company, as part of his vision for economic independence from white employers (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that nativism was the main cause of restrictions on immigration and civil liberties in 1920s America? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that assesses nativism alongside other causes (fear of Communism/anarchism from the Red Scare, economic competition, post-war anxiety); uses specific evidence for each (National Origins Act 1924 for nativism; Palmer Raids and Sacco and Vanzetti for Red Scare; Emergency Quota Act 1921 for economic pressure); engages with at least one interpretation. Secure: Clear argument addressing multiple causes with relevant evidence. Developing: Some awareness of multiple causes with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of the Red Scare in 1920s America. Interpretation A argues it was a genuine response to a real threat of Communist subversion. Interpretation B argues it was primarily a tool for targeting immigrants, minorities, and political dissenters. How far do the interpretations differ, and what might explain their differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies key differences (genuine security threat vs. manufactured hysteria, targeting criteria); uses own knowledge to evaluate both (post-Russian Revolution context, 1919 bombings for A; Palmer Raids abuses, Sacco and Vanzetti, deportation of thousands without evidence for B); explains why interpretations differ (political perspective, evidence base, proximity to events). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Identifies some differences and supports one. Emerging: Summarises each without explaining differences.

knowledge_checks.q: What was J. Edgar Hoover's role during the Palmer Raids?
options: Attorney General who ordered the raids
Head of the General Intelligence Division compiling files on radicals

knowledge_checks.q: The National Origins Act of 1924 used which year's census to calculate immigration quotas?
Sacco and Vanzetti were executed on 23 August _____, despite international protests.
Marcus Garvey's organisation, the _____, promoted Black pride, economic self-sufficiency, and an African homeland.
Match each figure to their role in the Red Scare and immigration era.
right: Attorney General who ordered mass raids on suspected radicals
Head of GID who compiled files on thousands of Americans
UNIA leader who promoted Back to Africa separatism

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Palmer Raids take place?
How many people were arrested in the January 1920 Palmer Raids?
Why were Sacco and Vanzetti arrested in 1920?
flashcard_questions.a: They were accused of murder during a payroll robbery in South Braintree, Massachusetts

flashcard_questions.q: How did Massachusetts officially recognise the injustice of the Sacco and Vanzetti case?
flashcard_questions.a: Governor Dukakis issued a 1977 proclamation condemning the prejudiced atmosphere surrounding the trial

flashcard_questions.q: What did the National Origins Act (1924) use the 1890 census for?
flashcard_questions.a: To set low quotas for countries whose immigration had grown after 1890 — targeting Southern and Eastern Europeans

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to Marcus Garvey in 1925-27?
flashcard_questions.a: Convicted of mail fraud in 1925, deported to Jamaica in 1927

flashcard_questions.q: What strategy did the NAACP use to fight discrimination?
flashcard_questions.a: Legal challenges, political lobbying, and publicity through The Crisis magazine

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Emergency Quota Act (1921)?
flashcard_questions.a: An earlier law limiting immigration, precursor to the stricter 1924 National Origins Act

glossary_terms.definition: Mass arrests of suspected radicals, anarchists, and Communists ordered by Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer between November 1919 and January 1920, which saw thousands detained, often without warrants, and hundreds deported.
Head of the General Intelligence Division during the Palmer Raids who compiled vast surveillance files on American citizens, later becoming the first director of the FBI.
Italian immigrants and anarchists arrested in 1920 for a murder during a robbery in Massachusetts and executed in 1927 despite widespread doubts about the fairness of their trial.

The 1924 immigration law (Johnson-Reed Act) that set strict quotas based on national origin, drastically limiting immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe and effectively banning immigration from Asia.
The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, which used legal challenges, political lobbying, and publicity campaigns against racial discrimination throughout the 1920s.

The Universal Negro Improvement Association, founded by Marcus Garvey, which promoted Black pride, economic self-sufficiency, and the vision of an independent African nation — offering a separatist alternative to the NAACP's integrationist strategy.
